claim: Amyloid-β (Aβ)-containing extracellular plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau-loaded intracellular neurofibrillary tangles are neuropathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Amyloid-β (Aβ)-containing extracellular plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau-loaded intracellular neurofibrillary tangles are neuropathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Alzheimer's disease research, representing the two major pathological features used to diagnose AD.

claim: Aβ exerts neuropathogenic activity through tau.
source: Although Aβ exerts neuropathogenic activity through tau, the mechanistic link between Aβ and tau pathology remains unknown.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, though the mechanism is stated to be unknown.

claim: The mechanistic link between Aβ and tau pathology remains unknown.
source: Although Aβ exerts neuropathogenic activity through tau, the mechanistic link between Aβ and tau pathology remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis is critical in Aβ1-42-induced tau pathology.
source: Here, we showed that the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis is critical in Aβ1-42-induced tau pathology.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fcgr2b knockout inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in AD mouse models.
source: Fcgr2b knockout or antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and related experiments.

claim: Antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in AD mouse models.
source: Fcgr2b knockout or antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and related experiments.

claim: Fcgr2b knockout rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
source: Fcgr2b knockout or antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
source: Fcgr2b knockout or antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody inhibited Aβ1-42-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and rescued memory impairments in AD mouse models.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: FcγRIIb phosphorylation at Tyr273 was found in AD brains.
source: FcγRIIb phosphorylation at Tyr273 was found in AD brains, in neuronal cells exposed to Aβ1-42, and recruited SHIP2 to form a protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from AD patient brain samples shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FcγRIIb phosphorylation at Tyr273 was found in neuronal cells exposed to Aβ1-42.
source: FcγRIIb phosphorylation at Tyr273 was found in AD brains, in neuronal cells exposed to Aβ1-42, and recruited SHIP2 to form a protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Phosphorylated FcγRIIb at Tyr273 recruited SHIP2 to form a protein complex.
source: FcγRIIb phosphorylation at Tyr273 was found in AD brains, in neuronal cells exposed to Aβ1-42, and recruited SHIP2 to form a protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Treatment with Aβ1-42 increased PtdIns(3,4)P2 levels from PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 to mediate tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: Consequently, treatment with Aβ1-42 increased PtdIns(3,4)P2 levels from PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 to mediate tau hyperphosphorylation.

claim: Targeting SHIP2 expression by lentiviral siRNA in 3xTg-AD mice rescued tau hyperphosphorylation.

claim: Targeting SHIP2 expression by lentiviral siRNA in 3xTg-AD mice rescued memory impairments.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SHIP2 rescued tau hyperphosphorylation in AD models.

claim: The FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis links Aβ neurotoxicity to tau pathology by dysregulating PtdIns(3,4)P2 metabolism.

evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the progressive loss of memory and neuronal degeneration.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the progressive loss of memory and the neuronal degeneration (Mattson, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Mattson, 2004.

claim: The pathological hallmarks of AD are the presence of senile plaques consisting of Aβ peptide and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) formed by abnormally hyperphosphorylated tau.
source: The pathological hallmarks of AD are the presence of senile plaques consisting of Aβ peptide and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) formed by abnormally hyperphosphorylated tau (Walsh and Selkoe, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Walsh and Selkoe, 2004.

claim: Aβ species are generated from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β- and γ-secretases.
source: Aβ species are generated from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β- and γ-secretases, and accumulate extracellularly (Haass and Selkoe, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Haass and Selkoe, 2007.

claim: Aβ species accumulate extracellularly.
source: Aβ species are generated from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β- and γ-secretases, and accumulate extracellularly (Haass and Selkoe, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Haass and Selkoe, 2007.

claim: Aβ contributes to AD pathology by exhibiting toxicity in susceptible neurons.
source: In general, Aβ contributes to AD pathology by exhibiting toxicity in susceptible neurons, facilitating tau hyperphosphorylation, disrupting proteasome activity, and triggering synaptic dysfunction (LaFerla et al., 2007; Kam et al., 2014).

claim: Aβ contributes to AD pathology by facilitating tau hyperphosphorylation.

claim: Tau is a microtubule-binding protein.
source: Tau is a microtubule-binding protein but dissociates from the microtubules and accumulates in neurons as it becomes highly phosphorylated at multiple sites, resulting in the impairment of microtubule assembly and function (Ballatore et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Ballatore et al., 2007.

claim: Tau dissociates from the microtubules and accumulates in neurons as it becomes highly phosphorylated at multiple sites.
source: Tau is a microtubule-binding protein but dissociates from the microtubules and accumulates in neurons as it becomes highly phosphorylated at multiple sites, resulting in the impairment of microtubule assembly and function (Ballatore et al., 2007).

claim: In the amyloid cascade hypothesis, tau is believed to be one of the major downstream targets of Aβ to produce neurotoxicity.
source: In the amyloid cascade hypothesis, tau is believed to be one of the major downstream targets of Aβ to produce neurotoxicity (Hardy and Selkoe, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the amyloid cascade hypothesis, supported by a citation to Hardy and Selkoe, 2002.

claim: Aβ accelerates neurodegeneration in neuronal cells but not in tau-deficient neurons.
source: Aβ accelerates neurodegeneration in neuronal cells but not in tau-deficient neurons (Rapoport et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rapoport et al., 2002.

claim: Tau depletion in mutant APP transgenic mice prevented Aβ pathologies, including learning and memory impairment.
source: Moreover, tau depletion in mutant APP transgenic mice prevented Aβ pathologies, including learning and memory impairment (Roberson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberson et al., 2007.

claim: Aβ immunization in 3xTg-AD mice reduced not only Aβ accumulation but also tau pathology.
source: The role of Aβ in tau pathology was also shown in 3xTg-AD mice expressing APP, presenilin, and tau transgenes in which Aβ immunization reduced not only Aβ accumulation but also tau pathology (Oddo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oddo et al., 2004.

claim: Higher levels of NFT have been observed in APPswe/P301L transgenic mice.
source: In addition, higher levels of NFT have been observed in APPswe/P301L transgenic mice (Lewis et al., 2001) and in 3xTg-AD mice (Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2001.

claim: Higher levels of NFT have been observed in 3xTg-AD mice.
source: In addition, higher levels of NFT have been observed in APPswe/P301L transgenic mice (Lewis et al., 2001) and in 3xTg-AD mice (Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oddo et al., 2003.

claim: Tau hyperphosphorylation is frequently found in AD brains.
source: More importantly, tau hyperphosphorylation is frequently found in AD brains (Grundke-Iqbal et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grundke-Iqbal et al., 1989.

claim: Tau kinases, such as glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), are activated by Aβ for tau phosphorylation in vitro and in vivo.
source: Apparently, tau kinases, such as glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), are activated by Aβ for tau phosphorylation in vitro and in vivo (Hoshi et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2006; Terwel et al., 2008; Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoshi et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2006; Terwel et al., 2008; Park et al., 2012.

claim: There is a pathologic signal pathway starting with extracellular Aβ and ending in the phosphorylation of intracellular tau.
source: All of these findings indicate the presence of a pathologic signal pathway starting with extracellular Aβ and ending in the phosphorylation of intracellular tau.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature.

claim: The mechanism connecting the two pathologic hallmarks of AD remains unknown.
source: However, the mechanism connecting the two pathologic hallmarks of AD remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Phosphoinositides play a major role in signal transduction upon cellular stimulation.
source: Phosphoinositides, the phosphorylated derivatives of phosphatidylinositol (PtdIns), such as PtdIns(3,4,5)P3, PtdIns(4,5)P2, and PtdIns(3,4)P2, are known to play a major role in signal transduction upon cellular stimulation (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006.

claim: The biological roles of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(4,5)P2 have been relatively well characterized in cell survival, proliferation, and synaptic function.
source: Among them, the biological roles of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(4,5)P2 have been relatively well characterized in cell survival, proliferation, and synaptic function via their binding proteins (Bunney and Katan, 2010; Khuong et al., 2013), but the function of PtdIns(3,4)P2 is largely unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bunney and Katan, 2010 and Khuong et al., 2013.

claim: The function of PtdIns(3,4)P2 is largely unknown.
source: Among them, the biological roles of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(4,5)P2 have been relatively well characterized in cell survival, proliferation, and synaptic function via their binding proteins (Bunney and Katan, 2010; Khuong et al., 2013), but the function of PtdIns(3,4)P2 is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 are formed when cells respond to signals.
source: Unlike PtdIns(4,5)P2, PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 are formed when cells respond to signals (Zhang and Majerus, 1998; Lemmon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Majerus, 1998 and Lemmon, 2008.

claim: SHIP removes 5′ phosphate from PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 to produce PtdIns(3,4)P2.
source: SH2 domain-containing phosphatidylinositol 5′-phosphatase (SHIP) removes 5′ phosphate from PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 to produce PtdIns(3,4)P2 (Damen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Damen et al., 1996.

claim: Phosphoinositide metabolism is dysregulated in AD.
source: Increasing evidence has revealed that phosphoinositide metabolism is dysregulated in AD; specifically, the level of PtdIns(4,5)P2 is decreased in human and mouse AD brains, and in the primary cortical neurons exposed to oligomeric Aβ (Stokes and Hawthorne, 1987; Jope et al., 1994; Berman et al., 2008), and recovery of PtdIns(4,5)P2 deficiency prevents AD-related cognitive deficits in mouse models (McIntire et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The level of PtdIns(4,5)P2 is decreased in human and mouse AD brains.
source: Increasing evidence has revealed that phosphoinositide metabolism is dysregulated in AD; specifically, the level of PtdIns(4,5)P2 is decreased in human and mouse AD brains, and in the primary cortical neurons exposed to oligomeric Aβ (Stokes and Hawthorne, 1987; Jope et al., 1994; Berman et al., 2008), and recovery of PtdIns(4,5)P2 deficiency prevents AD-related cognitive deficits in mouse models (McIntire et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).

claim: The hippocampus of 3xTg-AD mice at nine months of age was plaque-free.
source: Because FcγRIIb itself did not affect Aβ levels in these mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and the hippocampus of 3xTg-AD mice at nine months of age was plaque-free (Hirata-Fukae et al., 2008), we next examined the role of FcγRIIb in tau pathology in the mouse brains.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hirata-Fukae et al., 2008.

claim: Pathologic hyperphosphorylation of tau detected by CP13, PHF1, and AT180 antibodies was increased in 3xTg-AD mice showing memory impairment.
source: As reported (Hirata-Fukae et al., 2008), the pathologic hyperphosphorylation of tau detected by CP13, PHF1, and AT180 antibodies was found to be increased in the 3xTg-AD mice showing memory impairment (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1H,I and a citation to Hirata-Fukae et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic deletion of Fcgr2b in 3xTg-AD mice abolished the hyperphosphorylation of tau.
source: In contrast, genetic deletion of Fcgr2b in 3xTg-AD mice abolished the hyperphosphorylation of tau.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: Tau phosphorylation was markedly elevated in the brains of 20 month-old 3xTg-AD mice compared to 6 month-old mice.
source: In the brains of 20 month-old 3xTg-AD mice harboring Aβ plaques, tau phosphorylation was markedly elevated as compared to 6 month-old mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: FcγRIIb deficiency prevented the hyperphosphorylation of tau in 15 month-old 3xTg-AD mice.
source: FcγRIIb deficiency also prevented the hyperphosphorylation of tau in 15 month-old 3xTg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), indicating that tau phosphorylation mediated by FcγRIIb occurs at the onset of the disease and lasts to the late stage.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: Tau phosphorylation mediated by FcγRIIb occurs at the onset of the disease and lasts to the late stage.
source: FcγRIIb deficiency also prevented the hyperphosphorylation of tau in 15 month-old 3xTg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), indicating that tau phosphorylation mediated by FcγRIIb occurs at the onset of the disease and lasts to the late stage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing FcγRIIb's effect on tau phosphorylation at different ages.

claim: Fcgr2b deficiency inhibited tau phosphorylation in hAPP-J20 mice.
source: Similarly, this inhibitory effect of Fcgr2b deficiency on tau phosphorylation was observed in another AD model, hAPP-J20 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F,G.

claim: FcγRIIb is crucial for tau hyperphosphorylation in AD model mice showing memory impairment.
source: These results indicate that FcγRIIb is crucial for tau hyperphosphorylation in AD model mice showing memory impairment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective data on FcγRIIb's role in tau phosphorylation and memory impairment.

claim: Addition of purified hFcγRIIb ectodomain to culture medium blocked Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in primary cortical neurons.
source: Compared to Aβ only-treated neurons, addition of the purified hFcγRIIb ectodomain (hFcγRIIb-ED) to culture medium blocked Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in primary cortical neurons (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Anti-FcγRIIb antibody (2.4G2) blocked the interaction between Aβ1-42 and HA-tagged FcγRIIb.
source: With the notion that both Aβ1-42 oligomers and immunoglobulin complexes share the same binding site on FcγRIIb (Kam et al., 2013), we found that the incubation of cultured cells with anti-FcγRIIb antibody (2.4G2) blocked the interaction between Aβ1-42 and HA-tagged FcγRIIb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation to Kam et al., 2013.

claim: 2.4G2 antibody selectively recognized FcγRIIb but did not crossreact with Aβ1-40 or Aβ1-42.
source: This antibody selectively recognized FcγRIIb but did not crossreact with Aβ1-40 or Aβ1-42 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment with 2.4G2 antibody drastically decreased Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in mouse primary cortical neurons in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Consistently, treatment with 2.4G2 antibody drastically decreased Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation in mouse primary cortical neurons in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The interaction between Aβ1-42 and FcγRIIb is an initial step for tau phosphorylation in cultured neurons.
source: These observations suggest that the interaction between Aβ1-42 and FcγRIIb is an initial step for tau phosphorylation in the cultured neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that blocking the interaction prevents tau phosphorylation.

claim: Coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued the deficits of spontaneous alternation behavior in mice.
source: Interestingly, coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued the deficits of spontaneous alternation behavior (Figure 2E), object recognition memory (Figure 2F), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by Y-maze test data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued object recognition memory deficits in mice.
source: Interestingly, coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued the deficits of spontaneous alternation behavior (Figure 2E), object recognition memory (Figure 2F), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued passive avoidance memory deficits in mice.
source: Interestingly, coinjection of Aβ1-42 and 2.4G2 antibodies significantly rescued the deficits of spontaneous alternation behavior (Figure 2E), object recognition memory (Figure 2F), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by passive avoidance test data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Injection with normal IgG did not exhibit inhibitory effects on memory impairment.
source: On the other hand, injection with normal immunoglobulin G (IgG) did not exhibit such inhibitory effects on memory impairment.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Tau phosphorylation was highly increased in the hippocampus of Aβ1-42-injected mice.
source: From western blot analysis, we found that tau phosphorylation was highly increased in the hippocampus of Aβ1-42-injected mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was abolished in the hippocampus by coinjection with 2.4G2 antibody.
source: In contrast, Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was abolished in the hippocampus by coinjection with 2.4G2 antibody, but not with IgG (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was not abolished by coinjection with IgG.
source: In contrast, Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was abolished in the hippocampus by coinjection with 2.4G2 antibody, but not with IgG (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The interaction between Aβ1-42 and FcγRIIb is essential for tau hyperphosphorylation and memory impairment in mice.
source: Thus, we found that the interaction between Aβ1-42 and FcγRIIb is essential for tau hyperphosphorylation and memory impairment in mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that blocking the interaction prevents both tau phosphorylation and memory impairment.

claim: Tau kinases, such as GSK3β and Cdk5, were activated for tau phosphorylation in cultured neurons by treatment with Aβ1-42.
source: As reported (Plattner et al., 2006), we found that tau kinases, such as GSK3β and Cdk5, were activated for tau phosphorylation in cultured neurons by treatment with Aβ1-42 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation to Plattner et al., 2006.

claim: Fcgr2b deficiency in primary cortical neurons abrogated the activation of GSK3β triggered by Aβ1-42.
source: Notably, Fcgr2b deficiency in primary cortical neurons abrogated the activation of GSK3β and tau phosphorylation triggered by Aβ1-42, but not that of Cdk5.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Fcgr2b deficiency in primary cortical neurons abrogated tau phosphorylation triggered by Aβ1-42.
source: Notably, Fcgr2b deficiency in primary cortical neurons abrogated the activation of GSK3β and tau phosphorylation triggered by Aβ1-42, but not that of Cdk5.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Fcgr2b deficiency did not abrogate Cdk5 activation triggered by Aβ1-42.
source: Notably, Fcgr2b deficiency in primary cortical neurons abrogated the activation of GSK3β and tau phosphorylation triggered by Aβ1-42, but not that of Cdk5.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Ectopic expression of FcγRIIb induced tau hyperphosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of FcγRIIb induced tau hyperphosphorylation, detected by PHF1, CP13, and AT180 antibodies, in both SH-SY5Y cells and primary cortical neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Ectopic expression of FcγRIIb induced tau hyperphosphorylation in primary cortical neurons.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of FcγRIIb induced tau hyperphosphorylation, detected by PHF1, CP13, and AT180 antibodies, in both SH-SY5Y cells and primary cortical neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Treatment with SB-415286, a GSK3β inhibitor, markedly prevented FcγRIIb-induced tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: Consistently, treatment with SB-415286, a GSK3β inhibitor, markedly prevented FcγRIIb-induced tau hyperphosphorylation at those epitopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E), whereas roscovitine, a Cdk5 inhibitor, did not affect tau phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E.

claim: Roscovitine, a Cdk5 inhibitor, did not affect FcγRIIb-induced tau phosphorylation.
source: Consistently, treatment with SB-415286, a GSK3β inhibitor, markedly prevented FcγRIIb-induced tau hyperphosphorylation at those epitopes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E), whereas roscovitine, a Cdk5 inhibitor, did not affect tau phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F.

claim: FcγRIIb transduces Aβ signal into neuronal cells to activate GSK3β for tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: These observations suggest that FcγRIIb transduces Aβ signal into the neuronal cells to activate GSK3β for tau hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on GSK3β activation and tau phosphorylation.

claim: Treatment with Aβ1-42 induced phosphorylation at Tyr273 within an ITIM in the cytosolic region of FcγRIIb in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: We next investigated the mechanism for FcγRIIb transduction of Aβ signal into the neurons for tau phosphorylation, and found that treatment with Aβ1-42 induced phosphorylation at Tyr273 within an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (ITIM) in the cytosolic region of FcγRIIb in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phosphorylation of FcγRIIb at Tyr273 was detected in Aβ-treated primary cortical neurons.
source: This phosphorylation of FcγRIIb was also detected in Aβ-treated primary cortical neurons, but not in Fcgr2b KO neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Phosphorylation of FcγRIIb at Tyr273 was not detected in Fcgr2b KO neurons treated with Aβ.
source: This phosphorylation of FcγRIIb was also detected in Aβ-treated primary cortical neurons, but not in Fcgr2b KO neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Addition of purified hFcγRIIb-ED protein prevented Aβ-induced phosphorylation of FcγRIIb-Tyr273 in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Further, addition of purified hFcγRIIb-ED protein prevented Aβ-induced phosphorylation of FcγRIIb-Tyr273 in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 3C), indicating that FcγRIIb is phosphorylated on Tyr273 after its interaction with Aβ1-42.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: FcγRIIb is phosphorylated on Tyr273 after its interaction with Aβ1-42.
source: Further, addition of purified hFcγRIIb-ED protein prevented Aβ-induced phosphorylation of FcγRIIb-Tyr273 in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 3C), indicating that FcγRIIb is phosphorylated on Tyr273 after its interaction with Aβ1-42.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that blocking the interaction prevents phosphorylation.

claim: Overexpression of FcγRIIb Y273F mutant blocked Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Moreover, overexpression of FcγRIIb Y273F mutant, which was not phosphorylated (Figure 3D), blocked Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity to the control level in SH-SY5Y cells, whereas FcγRIIb WT potentiated it (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), indicating that FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation is required for Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FcγRIIb WT potentiated Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Moreover, overexpression of FcγRIIb Y273F mutant, which was not phosphorylated (Figure 3D), blocked Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity to the control level in SH-SY5Y cells, whereas FcγRIIb WT potentiated it (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), indicating that FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation is required for Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation is required for Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity.
source: Moreover, overexpression of FcγRIIb Y273F mutant, which was not phosphorylated (Figure 3D), blocked Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity to the control level in SH-SY5Y cells, whereas FcγRIIb WT potentiated it (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), indicating that FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation is required for Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that the non-phosphorylatable mutant blocks neurotoxicity.

claim: Reconstitution of Fcgr2b KO primary cortical neurons with FcγRIIb WT recovered Aβ-induced hyperphosphorylation of tau.
source: Unlike that in Fcgr2b-deficient neurons, reconstitution of the Fcgr2b KO primary cortical neurons with FcγRIIb WT recovered Aβ-induced hyperphosphorylation of tau, detected by PHF1, CP13, AT180, and 12E8 antibodies, as seen in WT neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Reconstitution with FcγRIIb-ΔCyto failed to show tau phosphorylation in response to Aβ1-42.
source: On the other hand, reconstitution with FcγRIIb-ΔCyto or FcγRIIb-Y273F failed to show tau phosphorylation at those epitopes in response to Aβ1-42 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Reconstitution with FcγRIIb-Y273F failed to show tau phosphorylation in response to Aβ1-42.
source: On the other hand, reconstitution with FcγRIIb-ΔCyto or FcγRIIb-Y273F failed to show tau phosphorylation at those epitopes in response to Aβ1-42 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The phosphorylation of FcγRIIb-Tyr273 by Aβ1-42 is critical for tau phosphorylation.
source: These results suggest that the phosphorylation of FcγRIIb-Tyr273 by Aβ1-42 is critical for tau phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reconstitution experiments showing that the Y273F mutant cannot restore tau phosphorylation.

claim: FcγRIIb phosphorylation on Tyr273 was found in the hippocampal tissues of five out of six AD patients (stage V and VI).
source: Even more interestingly, when we analyzed the phosphorylation status of FcγRIIb in the brains of AD patients, we found FcγRIIb phosphorylation on Tyr273 in the hippocampal tissues of five out of six AD patients (stage V and VI), but not in normal and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) patients (stage III) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from human brain samples shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FcγRIIb phosphorylation on Tyr273 was not found in normal and MCI patients (stage III).
source: Even more interestingly, when we analyzed the phosphorylation status of FcγRIIb in the brains of AD patients, we found FcγRIIb phosphorylation on Tyr273 in the hippocampal tissues of five out of six AD patients (stage V and VI), but not in normal and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) patients (stage III) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from human brain samples shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Tau phosphorylation at PHF was observed in four out of five AD patients with FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation-positive brains.
source: In addition, tau phosphorylation at PHF was observed in four out of the five AD patients with FcγRIIb-Tyr273 phosphorylation-positive brains.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from human brain samples shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The expression level of FcγRIIb was increased in AD brains.
source: As we previously reported, the expression level of FcγRIIb was increased in AD brains (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and previous reports.

claim: The phosphorylation of FcγRIIb found in AD brains is associated with tau phosphorylation and neuronal loss during AD pathogenesis.
source: With the notion that FcγRIIb phosphorylation is required for tau phosphorylation and Aβ1-42 neurotoxicity, it is likely that the phosphorylation of FcγRIIb found in AD brains is associated with tau phosphorylation and neuronal loss during AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and the observation of FcγRIIb phosphorylation in AD brains.

claim: SHIP2 is highly expressed in the brain.
source: Given that SHIP2 is highly expressed in the brain and SHIP1 is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic cells (Astle et al., 2007), we focused on SHIP2 and examined its ability to bind to phosphorylated FcγRIIb in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Astle et al., 2007.

claim: SHIP1 is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic cells.
source: Given that SHIP2 is highly expressed in the brain and SHIP1 is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic cells (Astle et al., 2007), we focused on SHIP2 and examined its ability to bind to phosphorylated FcγRIIb in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Astle et al., 2007.

claim: Overexpressed FcγRIIb-GFP bound to SHIP2-His in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation assays revealed that overexpressed FcγRIIb-GFP bound to SHIP2-His in SH-SY5Y cells, whereas the phospho-defective FcγRIIb (Y273F) mutant failed to do so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The phospho-defective FcγRIIb (Y273F) mutant failed to bind to SHIP2-His in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation assays revealed that overexpressed FcγRIIb-GFP bound to SHIP2-His in SH-SY5Y cells, whereas the phospho-defective FcγRIIb (Y273F) mutant failed to do so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a drastic increase in the binding between endogenous SHIP2 and FcγRIIb in SH-SY5Y cells after exposure to Aβ1-42.
source: Interestingly, compared to the lack of or weak interaction in untreated control cells, we found a drastic increase in the binding between endogenous SHIP2 and FcγRIIb in SH-SY5Y cells after exposure to Aβ1-42 (Figure 4C,D), suggesting that SHIP2 binds to FcγRIIb in neuronal cells in response to Aβ1-42.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: SHIP2 binds to FcγRIIb in neuronal cells in response to Aβ1-42.
source: Interestingly, compared to the lack of or weak interaction in untreated control cells, we found a drastic increase in the binding between endogenous SHIP2 and FcγRIIb in SH-SY5Y cells after exposure to Aβ1-42 (Figure 4C,D), suggesting that SHIP2 binds to FcγRIIb in neuronal cells in response to Aβ1-42.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Treatment of SH-SY5Y cells with Aβ1-42 enhanced subcellular localization of SHIP2 to the plasma membrane.
source: Treatment of SH-SY5Y cells with Aβ1-42 enhanced subcellular localization of SHIP2 to the plasma membrane and thus colocalization of SHIP2 with FcγRIIb (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Treatment of SH-SY5Y cells with Aβ1-42 enhanced colocalization of SHIP2 with FcγRIIb.
source: Treatment of SH-SY5Y cells with Aβ1-42 enhanced subcellular localization of SHIP2 to the plasma membrane and thus colocalization of SHIP2 with FcγRIIb (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SHIP2 was enriched in the membrane fraction following Aβ1-42 treatment.
source: In addition, subcellular fractionation assays revealed similar results, showing that SHIP2 was enriched in the membrane fraction following Aβ1-42 treatment, while it was detected in both the cytosol and membrane fractions in untreated control cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SHIP2 expression was not changed by Aβ1-42 treatment in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: However, SHIP2 expression was not changed by Aβ1-42 treatment in SH-SY5Y cells and in the brains of MCI and AD patients (Figure 4F andFigure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SHIP2 expression was not changed in the brains of MCI and AD patients.
source: However, SHIP2 expression was not changed by Aβ1-42 treatment in SH-SY5Y cells and in the brains of MCI and AD patients (Figure 4F andFigure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SHIP2 is recruited to the membrane to interact with FcγRIIb in neuronal cells following Aβ1-42 treatment.
source: Overall, our data indicates that SHIP2 is recruited to the membrane to interact with FcγRIIb in neuronal cells following Aβ1-42 treatment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on SHIP2 localization and interaction with FcγRIIb.

claim: The amount of TAPP1-PH-interacting PtdIns(3,4)P2 was increased in SH-SY5Y cells following exposure to Aβ1-42.
source: From the PLO assays using total lipid extracts, we found that the amount of TAPP1-PH-interacting PtdIns(3,4)P2 was increased in SH-SY5Y cells following exposure to Aβ1-42 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no increase in TAPP1-PH-interacting PtdIns(3,4)P2 by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, there was no such increase by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B or SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no increase in TAPP1-PH-interacting PtdIns(3,4)P2 by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, there was no such increase by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B or SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amount of GRP1-PH-interacting lipids was reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Conversely, the amount of the general receptor for phosphoinositides-1 (GRP1)-PH-interacting lipids, mainly PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 (Guillou et al., 2007), was reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y cells, but not in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B or SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and a citation to Guillou et al., 2007.

claim: The amount of GRP1-PH-interacting lipids was not reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B knockdown cells.
source: Conversely, the amount of the general receptor for phosphoinositides-1 (GRP1)-PH-interacting lipids, mainly PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 (Guillou et al., 2007), was reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y cells, but not in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B or SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amount of GRP1-PH-interacting lipids was not reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells.
source: Conversely, the amount of the general receptor for phosphoinositides-1 (GRP1)-PH-interacting lipids, mainly PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 (Guillou et al., 2007), was reduced by Aβ1-42 in SH-SY5Y cells, but not in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B or SH-SY5Y/INPPL1 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Similar patterns of changes in the levels of TAPP1-PH-interacting or GRP1-PH-interacting lipids were observed in WT primary cortical neurons after treatment with Aβ1-42.
source: Similar patterns of changes in the levels of TAPP1-PH-interacting or GRP1-PH-interacting lipids were also observed in WT primary cortical neurons after treatment with Aβ1-42 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Changes in TAPP1-PH-interacting or GRP1-PH-interacting lipids were not observed in Fcgr2b KO neurons after treatment with Aβ1-42.
source: Consistently, these changes were not observed in Fcgr2b KO neurons.
evidence: This is supported by PLO assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Phosphoinositide metabolism is affected by the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
source: These results indicate that phosphoinositide metabolism is affected by the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that knockdown of FcγRIIb or SHIP2 prevents Aβ-induced changes in phosphoinositide levels.

claim: The levels of PtdIns(3,4)P2 were increased by 30% in primary cortical neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42.
source: When we directly measured the levels of phosphoinositides with an ELISA assay, we observed that the levels of PtdIns(3,4)P2 were increased by 30% in primary cortical neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42, whereas PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 was decreased by 17% (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 was decreased by 17% in primary cortical neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42.
source: When we directly measured the levels of phosphoinositides with an ELISA assay, we observed that the levels of PtdIns(3,4)P2 were increased by 30% in primary cortical neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42, whereas PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 was decreased by 17% (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fcgr2b-deficiency abrogated changes in PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 levels induced by Aβ1-42.
source: However, Fcgr2b-deficiency abrogated these changes in PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P2 levels.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The levels of PtdIns(4,5)P2 were lowered by Aβ1-42 in WT neurons.
source: On the other hand, the levels of PtdIns(4,5)P2 were lowered by Aβ1-42 in WT neurons, consistent with a previous report (Berman et al., 2008), and also in FcgR2b KO neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Berman et al., 2008.

claim: The levels of PtdIns(4,5)P2 were lowered by Aβ1-42 in FcgR2b KO neurons.
source: On the other hand, the levels of PtdIns(4,5)P2 were lowered by Aβ1-42 in WT neurons, consistent with a previous report (Berman et al., 2008), and also in FcgR2b KO neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with Aβ1-42 enhanced the fluorescence of TAPP1-PH-GFP and concentrated it at the plasma membrane in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: While TAPP1-PH-GFP was found in a diffuse pattern in the cytosol of untreated SH-SY5Y cells, treatment with Aβ1-42 enhanced the fluorescence of TAPP1-PH-GFP and concentrated it at the plasma membrane (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Aβ-induced accumulation of TAPP1-PH-GFP at the plasma membrane was impaired in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, Aβ-induced accumulation of TAPP1-PH-GFP at the plasma membrane was impaired in SH-SY5Y/FCGR2B knockdown cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide induced membrane localization of TAPP1-PH-GFP in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: As reported (Cheung et al., 2007), hydrogen peroxide also induced membrane localization of TAPP1-PH-GFP in SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cheung et al., 2007.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide-induced membrane localization of TAPP1-PH-GFP was not affected by Fcgr2b deficiency.
source: However, this localization was not affected by Fcgr2b deficiency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aβ1-42 selectively dysregulates PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 levels in neurons via FcγRIIb.
source: These observations further support the idea that Aβ1-42 selectively dysregulates PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 levels in neurons via FcγRIIb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that FcγRIIb is required for Aβ-induced changes in these specific phosphoinositides but not PtdIns(4,5)P2.

claim: Treatment with PtdIns(3,4)P2 increased tau phosphorylation in primary cortical neurons in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Compared to untreated control cells, treatment with PtdIns(3,4)P2 increased tau phosphorylation (AT180, CP13, PHF1) in primary cortical neurons in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The increase in tau hyperphosphorylation was specific to PtdIns(3,4)P2.
source: Interestingly, the increase in tau hyperphosphorylation was specific to PtdIns(3,4)P2; other phosphoinositides, such as PtdIns(4,5)P2, PtdIns(3,5)P2, and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3, failed to do so.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 treatment reduced the inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β at Ser9 in neurons.
source: Consistent with the activation of GSK3β by Aβ1-42, PtdIns(3,4)P2 treatment also reduced the inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β at Ser9 in neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 induced the expression of GRP78, a typical marker of unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Moreover, PtdIns(3,4)P2 induced the expression of GRP78, a typical marker of unfolded protein response (UPR), as well (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2-induced GSK3β activation and tau phosphorylation were attenuated by treatment with ER stress inhibitors.
source: We further found that PtdIns(3,4)P2-induced GSK3β activation and tau phosphorylation were attenuated by the treatment with ER stress inhibitors, such as 4-PBA and Salubrinal, a chemical chaperone and an eIF2α dephosphorylation inhibitor, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ER stress response and GSK3β activation triggered by Aβ were declined by a SHIP2 inhibitor AS1949490.
source: We confirmed that ER stress response and GSK3β activation triggered by Aβ were all declined by a SHIP2 inhibitor AS1949490 or lentiviral expression of Inppl1 siRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: ER stress response and GSK3β activation triggered by Aβ were declined by lentiviral expression of Inppl1 siRNA.
source: We confirmed that ER stress response and GSK3β activation triggered by Aβ were all declined by a SHIP2 inhibitor AS1949490 or lentiviral expression of Inppl1 siRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: An increase in the PtdIns(3,4)P2 level by Aβ1-42 activates GSK3β through ER stress for tau hyperphosphorylation in neuronal cells.
source: Combined with the previous study showing that ER stress stimulates GSK3β activity (Ren et al., 2015), these results suggest that an increase in the PtdIns(3,4)P2 level by Aβ1-42 activates GSK3β through ER stress for tau hyperphosphorylation in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and a citation to Ren et al., 2015.

claim: Knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells abrogated tau phosphorylation by Aβ1-42.
source: Unlike enhanced tau phosphorylation by Aβ1-42 in control cells, knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells abrogated tau phosphorylation by Aβ1-42 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of SHIP2 alone was sufficient to increase tau hyperphosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Conversely, overexpression of SHIP2 alone was sufficient to increase tau hyperphosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: An activity-dead SHIP2 mutant with Asp608 replaced by Ala did not increase tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: On the other hand, these effects were not observed using an activity-dead SHIP2 mutant with Asp608 replaced by Ala (Nakatsu et al., 2010) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and a citation to Nakatsu et al., 2010.

claim: Neuronal cell death triggered by Aβ1-42 treatment was greatly reduced by knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: In addition, neuronal cell death triggered by Aβ1-42 treatment or FcγRIIb overexpression was greatly reduced by knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Neuronal cell death triggered by FcγRIIb overexpression was greatly reduced by knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: In addition, neuronal cell death triggered by Aβ1-42 treatment or FcγRIIb overexpression was greatly reduced by knockdown of SHIP2 expression in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: SHIP2 is a key signal mediator of FcγRIIb in Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and neurotoxicity.
source: Together, these data suggest that SHIP2 is a key signal mediator of FcγRIIb in Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that SHIP2 is required for FcγRIIb-mediated effects.

claim: Infection with lenti-siInppl1 reduced SHIP2 levels in HT22 cells.
source: We confirmed that infection with lenti-siInppl1 reduced SHIP2 levels in both HT22 cells and primary cortical neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Infection with lenti-siInppl1 reduced SHIP2 levels in primary cortical neurons.
source: We confirmed that infection with lenti-siInppl1 reduced SHIP2 levels in both HT22 cells and primary cortical neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Infection with lenti-siInppl1 abrogated Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation in primary cortical neurons.
source: Consistently, we observed that infection with lenti-siInppl1 abrogated Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation (PHF1, CP13) in primary cortical neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg AD mice showed no significant memory deficits in Y-maze test.
source: When we stereotaxically injected lenti-siInppl1 into the dentate gyrus of WT and 3xTg-AD mice, we observed that compared to control 3xTg AD mice, lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg AD mice showed no significant memory deficits in Y-maze and novel object recognition tests at 20 days after viral injection (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Y-maze test data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg AD mice showed no significant memory deficits in novel object recognition test.
source: When we stereotaxically injected lenti-siInppl1 into the dentate gyrus of WT and 3xTg-AD mice, we observed that compared to control 3xTg AD mice, lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg AD mice showed no significant memory deficits in Y-maze and novel object recognition tests at 20 days after viral injection (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Tau phosphorylation was reduced in the hippocampi of lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg-AD mice.
source: When we also monitored tau phosphorylation and SHIP2 levels in brains by western blot analysis, we found that tau phosphorylation and SHIP2 levels were reduced in the hippocampi of lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg-AD mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SHIP2 levels were reduced in the hippocampi of lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg-AD mice.
source: When we also monitored tau phosphorylation and SHIP2 levels in brains by western blot analysis, we found that tau phosphorylation and SHIP2 levels were reduced in the hippocampi of lenti-siInppl1-injected 3xTg-AD mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SHIP2 is critical to memory impairment and tau hyperphosphorylation in 3xTg-AD mice.
source: These results indicate that SHIP2 is critical to memory impairment and tau hyperphosphorylation in 3xTg-AD mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that SHIP2 knockdown rescues memory impairment and tau phosphorylation.

claim: Treatment of primary cortical neurons with AS1949490 inhibited Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: Treatment of primary cortical neurons with AS1949490 inhibited Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and neuronal cell death (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Treatment of primary cortical neurons with AS1949490 inhibited Aβ-induced neuronal cell death.
source: Treatment of primary cortical neurons with AS1949490 inhibited Aβ-induced tau hyperphosphorylation and neuronal cell death (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of spatial working memory in mice.
source: Behavioral tests following the i.c.v. injection of sub-lethal doses of Aβ1-42 and AS1949490 revealed that AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of spatial working memory (Figure 6F), object recognition memory (Figure 6G), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by Y-maze test data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of object recognition memory in mice.
source: Behavioral tests following the i.c.v. injection of sub-lethal doses of Aβ1-42 and AS1949490 revealed that AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of spatial working memory (Figure 6F), object recognition memory (Figure 6G), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of passive avoidance memory in mice.
source: Behavioral tests following the i.c.v. injection of sub-lethal doses of Aβ1-42 and AS1949490 revealed that AS1949490 significantly rescued Aβ1-42-induced impairments of spatial working memory (Figure 6F), object recognition memory (Figure 6G), and passive avoidance memory (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by passive avoidance test data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: AS1949490 suppressed Aβ1-42-induced tau phosphorylation in mouse hippocampal tissues.
source: Moreover, from western blot analysis of the mouse hippocampal tissues, we found that AS1949490 suppressed Aβ1-42-induced tau phosphorylation (PHF1, CP13, AT180) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of SHIP2 is amenable to the development of AD therapeutics targeting Aβ1-42-induced tau phosphorylation and memory impairment.
source: Taken together, these observations support the view that pharmacological manipulation of SHIP2 is amenable to the development of AD therapeutics targeting Aβ1-42-induced tau phosphorylation and memory impairment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that SHIP2 inhibition rescues tau phosphorylation and memory impairment.

claim: This is the first study showing crucial mediator, the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis, which is responsible for Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation, memory impairment, and neuronal loss in AD models.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study showing crucial mediator, the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis, which is responsible for Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation, memory impairment, and neuronal loss in AD models.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The selective interaction of oligomeric Aβ1-42 with FcγRIIb may hint at why Aβ1-42, but not Aβ1-40, is important in tau pathology.
source: Because the interaction of Aβ species, especially oligomeric Aβ1-42, with FcγRIIb accounts for such neuropathogenic defects of AD as an initiation step, the selective interaction of oligomeric Aβ1-42 with FcγRIIb may hint at why Aβ1-42, but not Aβ1-40, is important in tau pathology (Oddo et al., 2008; Kam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the study's findings and citations to Oddo et al., 2008 and Kam et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of the interaction between FcγRIIb and Aβ using anti-FcγRIIb antibody prevents Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation and memory deficits.
source: Consequently, inhibition of the interaction between FcγRIIb and Aβ using anti-FcγRIIb antibody prevents Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation and memory deficits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: FcγRIIb plays a crucial role in tau phosphorylation and neurotoxicity in vitro and in vivo in response to different species of Aβ oligomers.
source: Nonetheless, we propose here that FcγRIIb plays a crucial role in tau phosphorylation and neurotoxicity in vitro and in vivo in response to these species of Aβ, probably a certain common species among the different sources of Aβ oligomers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's use of multiple sources of Aβ oligomers.

claim: Microglia was activated in 3xTg-AD mice and this activation was reduced significantly in the cortex by FcγRIIb deficiency.
source: As expected, we observed that microglia was activated in 3xTg-AD mice and this activation was also reduced significantly in the cortex and marginally in the hippocampus by FcγRIIb deficiency (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Microglia activation was reduced marginally in the hippocampus by FcγRIIb deficiency in 3xTg-AD mice.
source: As expected, we observed that microglia was activated in 3xTg-AD mice and this activation was also reduced significantly in the cortex and marginally in the hippocampus by FcγRIIb deficiency (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Both FcγRIIb mRNA and protein are expressed in neurons.
source: Recently, however, we and other colleagues identified that both FcγRIIb mRNA and protein are also expressed in neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Cahoy et al., 2008; Suemitsu et al., 2010; Kam et al., 2013), though FcγRIIb expression in neurons is low compared to astrocytes and immune tissues.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to Cahoy et al., 2008; Suemitsu et al., 2010; Kam et al., 2013.

claim: FcγRIIb expression in neurons is low compared to astrocytes and immune tissues.
source: Recently, however, we and other colleagues identified that both FcγRIIb mRNA and protein are also expressed in neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Cahoy et al., 2008; Suemitsu et al., 2010; Kam et al., 2013), though FcγRIIb expression in neurons is low compared to astrocytes and immune tissues.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative expression levels of FcγRIIb.

claim: FcγRIIb expression is increased several folds in primary neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42.
source: Notably, its expression is increased at least several folds in primary neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42 and in AD brain (Kam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kam et al., 2013.

claim: FcγRIIb expression is increased in AD brain.
source: Notably, its expression is increased at least several folds in primary neurons after exposure to Aβ1-42 and in AD brain (Kam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kam et al., 2013 and data in Figure 3F.

claim: Transgenic expression of the FcγRIIb mutant lacking its cytoplasmic domain in neurons blocked memory impairment in 3xTg AD mice.
source: In addition, transgenic expression of the FcγRIIb mutant lacking its cytoplasmic domain in the neurons blocked memory impairment in 3xTg AD mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by FcγRIIb deficiency in primary cultured neurons.
source: Moreover, the results showing that Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by FcγRIIb deficiency, antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody, or SHIP2 inhibitor in primary cultured neurons assure neuronal function of the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 6.

claim: Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody in primary cultured neurons.
source: Moreover, the results showing that Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by FcγRIIb deficiency, antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody, or SHIP2 inhibitor in primary cultured neurons assure neuronal function of the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by SHIP2 inhibitor in primary cultured neurons.
source: Moreover, the results showing that Aβ-induced tau phosphorylation was prevented by FcγRIIb deficiency, antagonistic FcγRIIb antibody, or SHIP2 inhibitor in primary cultured neurons assure neuronal function of the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The inflammation mediated by FcγRIIb in 3xTg-AD mice is not likely a major cause of the memory impairment but contributes to the aggravation of memory impairment in the mice.
source: Together, we believe that the inflammation mediated by FcγRIIb in 3xTg-AD mice is not likely a major cause of the memory impairment but contributes to the aggravation of memory impairment in the mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on neuronal function of FcγRIIb and the observation of reduced microglial activation.

claim: FcγRIIb acts as an inhibitory receptor in B cells.
source: Unlike other FcγRs that have an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activating motif (ITAM), FcγRIIb has a unique ITIM in its cytoplasmic tail and thus acts as an inhibitory receptor in B cells (Okun et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Okun et al., 2010.

claim: The binding of extracellular Aβ1-42 to FcγRIIb induces phosphorylation in the ITIM of FcγRIIb in neuronal cells.
source: Excitingly, the binding of extracellular Aβ1-42 to FcγRIIb induces phosphorylation in the ITIM of FcγRIIb in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Lyn kinase is expressed in neurons.
source: We observed that Lyn kinase is expressed in neurons and that knockdown of LYN expression blocks Aβ-induced FcγRIIb phosphorylation and neurotoxicity (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Knockdown of LYN expression blocks Aβ-induced FcγRIIb phosphorylation.
source: We observed that Lyn kinase is expressed in neurons and that knockdown of LYN expression blocks Aβ-induced FcγRIIb phosphorylation and neurotoxicity (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Knockdown of LYN expression blocks Aβ-induced neurotoxicity.
source: We observed that Lyn kinase is expressed in neurons and that knockdown of LYN expression blocks Aβ-induced FcγRIIb phosphorylation and neurotoxicity (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation but the data is not shown.

claim: Lyn phosphorylates the ITIM of FcγRIIb in neuronal cells in response to Aβ1-42.
source: Thus, it is likely that Lyn phosphorylates the ITIM of FcγRIIb in neuronal cells in response to Aβ1-42.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on Lyn expression and its role in FcγRIIb phosphorylation.

claim: The phosphorylation of PirB is not associated with Aβ signaling.
source: In the case of PirB that shares structural similarity with FcγRIIb and also acts as an Aβ receptor for synaptic plasticity, the phosphorylation of PirB is not associated with Aβ signaling (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: FcγRIIb facilitates tau phosphorylation and neuronal loss in AD brains.
source: Thus, we believe that FcγRIIb facilitates tau phosphorylation and neuronal loss in AD brains, consistent with the proposed role of tau in AD pathogenesis, such as severe memory impairment and neuronal loss (Ballatore et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings and a citation to Ballatore et al., 2007.

claim: SHIP2 is a key mediator in delivering the toxic signal of Aβ1-42 to tau by binding to the phosphorylated FcγRIIb.
source: Interestingly, we show that SHIP2 is a key mediator in delivering the toxic signal of Aβ1-42 to tau by binding to the phosphorylated FcγRIIb.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Inppl1 transgenic mice show impaired insulin signaling and glucose intolerance.
source: Inppl1 transgenic mice show impaired insulin signaling and glucose intolerance, while Inppl1 KO mice are highly resistant to weight gain on a high-fat diet (Sleeman et al., 2005; Kagawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sleeman et al., 2005 and Kagawa et al., 2008.

claim: Inppl1 KO mice are highly resistant to weight gain on a high-fat diet.
source: Inppl1 transgenic mice show impaired insulin signaling and glucose intolerance, while Inppl1 KO mice are highly resistant to weight gain on a high-fat diet (Sleeman et al., 2005; Kagawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sleeman et al., 2005 and Kagawa et al., 2008.

claim: Targeting SHIP2 is thought to be a promising approach for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.
source: Thus, targeting SHIP2 is thought to be a promising approach for the treatment of other diseases, including type 2 diabetes (Vanhanen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanhanen et al., 2006.

claim: Metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance and glucose intolerance, is highly associated with AD.
source: Given that metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance and glucose intolerance, is highly associated with AD (Vanhanen et al., 2006; Razay et al., 2007), we speculate that SHIP2 may play a dual role in AD and diabetes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanhanen et al., 2006 and Razay et al., 2007.

claim: SHIP2 may play a dual role in AD and diabetes.
source: Given that metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance and glucose intolerance, is highly associated with AD (Vanhanen et al., 2006; Razay et al., 2007), we speculate that SHIP2 may play a dual role in AD and diabetes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the association between metabolic syndrome and AD.

claim: A SHIP2 inhibitor exhibited an ameliorating effect on the impaired memory function of diabetic mice.
source: In support of this, a SHIP2 inhibitor exhibited an ameliorating effect on the impaired memory function of diabetic mice (Soeda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soeda et al., 2010.

claim: Several single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of SHIP2 are involved in metabolic syndrome.
source: Several single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of SHIP2 are involved in metabolic syndrome (Kaisaki et al., 2004; Kagawa et al., 2005); thus, it will be very interesting to evaluate the effect of these SHIP2 SNPs on AD pathogenesis in our FcγRIIb-SHIP2 axis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaisaki et al., 2004 and Kagawa et al., 2005.

claim: Dysregulation of phosphoinositide metabolism is increasingly recognized as important in various diseases, such as cancer, diabetes, and myopathy.
source: Dysregulation of phosphoinositide metabolism is increasingly recognized as important in various diseases, such as cancer, diabetes, and myopathy (Wymann and Schneiter, 2008; Kok et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wymann and Schneiter, 2008 and Kok et al., 2009.

claim: The phosphoinositide pool is altered in AD.
source: The phosphoinositide pool is also altered in AD (Stokes and Hawthorne, 1987; Jope et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stokes and Hawthorne, 1987 and Jope et al., 1994.

claim: A change in the PtdIns(3,4)P2 level is implicated in AD pathogenesis through tau hyperphosphorylation.
source: In particular, this work shows that a change in the PtdIns(3,4)P2 level is implicated in AD pathogenesis through tau hyperphosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 is scarce under normal conditions and increases through signaling.
source: PtdIns(3,4)P2 is scarce under normal conditions and increases through signaling (Lemmon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lemmon, 2008.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 have distinct roles in neurodegeneration.
source: While PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 are known to overlap to some degree in their functions, they apparently have distinct roles in neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about the distinct roles of these phosphoinositides.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2, but not PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(4,5)P2, potentiates glutamate-induced cell death in neurons.
source: Recently, it was shown that PtdIns(3,4)P2, but not PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(4,5)P2, potentiates glutamate-induced cell death in neurons (Sasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 2010.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 phosphatase INPP4A deficiency shows increased level of PtdIns(3,4)P2 and leads to neurodegeneration in brains.
source: In addition, PtdIns(3,4)P2 phosphatase INPP4A deficiency shows increased level of PtdIns(3,4)P2 and leads to neurodegeneration in brains (Sasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 2010.

claim: PtdIns(3,4)P2 selectively induces tau hyperphosphorylation in neurons.
source: We also observed that PtdIns(3,4)P2 selectively induces tau hyperphosphorylation in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PTEN dephosphorylates PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 at position 3 and generates PtdIns(4,5)P2.
source: In addition, tensin homolog deletion on chromosome 10 (PTEN) also dephosphorylates PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 at position 3 and generates PtdIns(4,5)P2 (Li et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Li et al., 1997.

claim: The reduced level of PTEN in AD brains correlates with an increase in tau phosphorylation.
source: The reduced level of PTEN in AD brains correlates with an increase in tau phosphorylation and, thus, dysregulation of PTEN also contributes to tau pathology (Kerr et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2006 and Zhang et al., 2006.

claim: Dysregulation of PTEN contributes to tau pathology.
source: The reduced level of PTEN in AD brains correlates with an increase in tau phosphorylation and, thus, dysregulation of PTEN also contributes to tau pathology (Kerr et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2006 and Zhang et al., 2006.

claim: Genetic reduction of synaptojanin 1 ameliorates behavioral and synaptic deficits in AD models.
source: More recently, genetic reduction of synaptojanin 1 (Synj1), the major PtdIns(4,5)P2 phosphatase in the brain, ameliorates behavioral and synaptic deficits and accelerates Aβ clearance through rescuing PtdIns(4,5)P2 deficiency (McIntire et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McIntire et al., 2012 and Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: Genetic reduction of synaptojanin 1 accelerates Aβ clearance through rescuing PtdIns(4,5)P2 deficiency.
source: More recently, genetic reduction of synaptojanin 1 (Synj1), the major PtdIns(4,5)P2 phosphatase in the brain, ameliorates behavioral and synaptic deficits and accelerates Aβ clearance through rescuing PtdIns(4,5)P2 deficiency (McIntire et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McIntire et al., 2012 and Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: Oligomeric Aβ decreases PtdIns(4,5)P2 levels in AD.
source: Because oligomeric Aβ decreases PtdIns(4,5)P2 levels in AD (Berman et al., 2008), as we also observed, there is a possibility that SHIP2 activation together with either Synj1 upregulation or PTEN downregulation induces the imbalance in the phosphoinositide pool between PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(4,5)P2, and leads to AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berman et al., 2008 and data in Figure 5C.

claim: SHIP2 activation together with either Synj1 upregulation or PTEN downregulation may induce the imbalance in the phosphoinositide pool between PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(4,5)P2, leading to AD pathogenesis.
source: Because oligomeric Aβ decreases PtdIns(4,5)P2 levels in AD (Berman et al., 2008), as we also observed, there is a possibility that SHIP2 activation together with either Synj1 upregulation or PTEN downregulation induces the imbalance in the phosphoinositide pool between PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(4,5)P2, and leads to AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the study's findings and the literature on phosphoinositide metabolism.

claim: The FcγRIIb-SHIP2 signaling axis provides the missing link between Aβ and tau pathologies.
source: In conclusion, the FcγRIIb-SHIP2 signaling axis provides the missing link between Aβ and tau pathologies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the collective experimental data.

claim: Aβ1-42 induces FcγRIIb phosphorylation to recruit SHIP2, leading to disruption of phosphoinositide metabolism for tau hyperphosphorylation and memory impairment in neurons and AD model mice.
source: Notably, Aβ1-42 induces FcγRIIb phosphorylation to recruit SHIP2, leading to disruption of phosphoinositide metabolism for tau hyperphosphorylation and memory impairment in neurons and AD model mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: Selective inhibition of the interaction between FcγRIIb and Aβ1-42 is a potential therapeutic approach for AD.
source: Together with the Aβ-lowering strategy, our results provide new ways for AD therapeutics to rescue Aβ and tau pathology: i) selective inhibition of the interaction between FcγRIIb and Aβ1-42, ii) inhibition of a kinase (i.e., Lyn) which phosphorylates FcγRIIb upon Aβ1-42 stimulation, and iii) inhibition of SHIP2 which disrupts phosphoinositide metabolism.
